newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Old Yeltsin foe makes comeback in regional election.
newsitem.headline: Old Yeltsin foe makes comeback in regional election.

text.p: Alexander Rutskoi, the former Russian vice-president who became a bitter enemy of Boris Yeltsin, completed a remarkable comeback on Monday by being elected governor of the central Kursk region by a landslide.

The victory of Rutskoi, who led a bloody rebellion against President Boris Yeltsin in 1993, was one of several setbacks for the Kremlin as results came in Monday from a series of regional elections held on Sunday.

Russian news agencies said Rutskoi, who had only two days to campaign, won 79 percent of the votes. Vasily Shuteyev, appointed by Yeltsin in 1991 and regional governor since then, finished second on just 18 percent.
The new post will give Rutskoi, 49, a place in the Federation Council, the upper chamber of parliament.

Rutskoi was Yeltsin's running mate when the Russian president was first elected in 1991. But they soon fell out personally and politically, and Rutskoi was jailed for leading the 1993 rebellion by hardline parliamentarians.
He was later pardoned and went back into politics, forming a nationalist movement allied with the opposition communists.
Sunday's polls were part of a series of elections which are gradually being held to elect the regional leaders who make up the Federation Council.
The Kremlin administration is watching the elections closely in the hope that its preferred candidates, mostly current governors nominated by Yeltsin, will consolidate their position.
But they face stiff opposition from contenders representing the National Patriotic Bloc led by the communists.

The communists hope to cash in on the hardships suffered under economic reforms to increase their representation in the Federation Council, where nearly half the 178 members still owe their jobs to Yeltsin.

The opposition already dominates the State Duma lower house. Winning control of the Federation Council would increase the opposition's ability to block government legislation and overturn presidential decrees or vetos.

Rutskoi was initially banned from running by the local electoral commission which said he could not run becasue he had moved out of Kursk his home region, long ago. But a court reinstated Rutskoi just two days before the poll.
Rutskoi's comeback is certain to infuriate the Kremlin.
"It is a serious defeat for democracy," said Sergei Belyaev, head of the pro-government Our Home is Russia Duma's faction.

Yeltsin chose the Afghan war hero as his running mate in 1991 to win over the votes of reformist communists and the military. But Rutskoi later took the side of the conservative parliament in a power struggle with the Russian leader.
When Yeltsin, putting the constitution aside, tried to dissolve parliament in September 1993, deputies refused to obey and proclaimed Rutskoi their president.

The moustachioed general led a bloody uprising in Moscow on October 3. Government tanks ended the protest by shelling the parliament building, Rutskoi and other opponents were jailed and the post of vice-president was scrapped.
The new parliament pardoned Rutskoi the following year. He went on to form the nationalist Derzhava movement which backed the communist candidate in this year's presidential election.
In other setbacks in Sunday's polls, an opposition member of parliament became governor in Kirov, a region east of Moscow.

Yeltsin's appointee was defeated in the western enclave of Kaliningrad, and the Pskov region will require a second round of voting. In one success for the Kremlin, the Yeltsin-backed candidate was elected on the far eastern island of Sakhalin.
Before Sunday, the score between the communists and the Kremlin in the regional elections was level.
